entities.name: Ahmad ibn Nizam al-Mulk
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Ḍiyaʾ al-Mulk Aḥmad ibn Niẓām al-Mulk, born unknown, died 1149, was a Persian vizier of the Seljuq Empire and then the Abbasid Caliphate. He was the son of Nizam al-Mulk, one of the most famous viziers of the Seljuq Empire.

As vizier, Ahmad ibn Nizam al-Mulk implemented administrative reforms, including the creation of a centralized bureaucracy and the establishment of a network of roads and caravanserais. He also promoted trade and commerce, and his policies helped to establish the Seljuq Empire as a major power in the region.

Ahmad ibn Nizam al-Mulk's significance extends beyond his own lifetime, as his reforms and policies had a lasting impact on the development of the Islamic world. His legacy can be seen in the continued use of the centralized bureaucracy he established, and his promotion of trade and commerce helped to lay the foundations for the growth of cities and trade networks in the Middle East and beyond.

One of the most striking aspects of Ahmad ibn Nizam al-Mulk's legacy is the enduring power of his administrative reforms. The concept of the 'diwan' - a centralized administrative body - has been adopted by many modern governments, including those in the Middle East and beyond. This is a testament to the enduring legacy of Ahmad ibn Nizam al-Mulk, who played a pivotal role in shaping the course of history in the Islamic world.

In 1149, Ahmad ibn Nizam al-Mulk died, leaving behind a legacy that continues to shape the world today. His commitment to the promotion of trade and commerce helped to lay the foundations for the growth of cities and trade networks in the Middle East and beyond, and his administrative reforms continue to be studied and emulated by scholars and policymakers around the world.
